lines: A pipeline's own dashboard reports a perfect month: every single run finished right on schedule.
Meanwhile, the customer-facing report that pipeline actually feeds was showing yesterday's numbers for several days straight.
A step downstream of the pipeline, a view meant to refresh right after, had silently stopped refreshing.
The dashboard wasn't lying. It was just measuring the wrong point entirely.
This course has already named six quality dimensions, more than once: how fresh something is, how complete, how valid, how unique, how consistent, how accurate.
Those definitions aren't new here, and they're only recapped briefly.
What's new is turning each one into an actual measured number, with an explicit target and a budget attached to it.
A feeling about quality becomes something you can page a person about.
Worth pausing before the reveal.
A pipeline can genuinely finish exactly on schedule, every time, while whatever a person actually looks at is still stale.
So where should a freshness measurement actually be taken?
At the pipeline's own finish line, or somewhere else entirely?
steps.answer: At the point a consumer actually reads the data -- a dashboard query, an API response -- not wherever the pipeline itself happens to finish writing.

lines: Here's that read point, named directly.
A freshness measurement taken where a consumer actually reads the data, not where the pipeline finishes writing it.
Those two points agree almost all the time, which is exactly why the gap is so easy to miss.
They stop agreeing the moment some downstream step, a cache or a view, quietly stops doing its job.
steps.takeaway: A pipeline finishing on time isn't the same claim as the data being fresh. Only the read point can tell the two apart.

lines: One more question worth asking before it's answered.
A table a customer looks at directly and a table used only for occasional internal exploration clearly don't carry the same weight if either one goes stale.
Should they really be held to the exact same freshness target anyway?
Or does the target itself need to depend on who's actually looking?
steps.answer: No, they shouldn't share one target. A table customers actually see earns a much tighter target than one used only for occasional internal digging.

lines: Here's how that's actually structured.
A top-tier, customer-facing table gets a noticeably tighter freshness target than a lower-tier, internal table.
Whatever slack that target leaves -- the gap between a perfect score and the target itself -- is called an error budget.
That slack gets spent on purpose, by things like a deliberate historical backfill or a planned schema change, not just lost to random failures.
steps.takeaway: An error budget is not a failure allowance. It is the slack a team is allowed to spend on purpose.

lines: Here's the alerting rule behind this, sourced directly from a well-known site-reliability engineering guide rather than invented for this course.
A short time window paired with a fast rate of budget being spent pages someone immediately.
A longer time window paired with a slower, but still meaningfully large, rate of spend doesn't need a page -- it opens a ticket instead.
Together, the two windows catch both a sudden, sharp failure and a slow, quiet one before either empties the whole budget unnoticed.
Pulling it together now.
Measure freshness at the point a consumer actually reads the data, not wherever the pipeline itself happens to finish.
Size the target by who's actually affected, spend the resulting budget on purpose rather than losing it to accidents, and alert on how fast that budget is draining.
The hook's dashboard wasn't wrong about its own number. It was simply answering a different question than the one that mattered.
steps.takeaway: The hook's dashboard wasn't lying. It was just measuring the wrong point in the pipeline.

lines: One real test to close on, run against an actual database rather than just described.
A full month of a real pipeline, measured at both points at once: right where it finishes, and right where a consumer would actually read from it.
The same downstream failure from the very start of this topic is injected partway through that month.
Does the finish-time measurement ever catch on, even late -- or does it stay perfect the entire time?
steps.answer: It stays perfect the entire time, because the pipeline genuinely never missed its own schedule once. Only the read-point measurement saw the failure, and the sourced ticket-alert rule fired exactly when the real numbers said it should.
